questions.question: On which elements does the z-index property work?
options: Positioned elements (relative, absolute, fixed, sticky) and direct flex/grid children
questions.explanation: z-index is only effective on positioned elements (relative, absolute, fixed, sticky) or flex/grid items.

questions.question: Why will an element with z-index: 9999 render behind an element with z-index: 2 if their parents have competing stacking contexts?
options: A child element cannot escape the stacking context of its parent
9999 exceeds the maximum 16-bit integer limit in CSS
Odd numbers always lose to even numbers in CSS
questions.hint: Parent stacking context limits child layering.
questions.explanation: If a parent element belongs to a lower stacking context, its children are locked inside and can never render above a higher parent stacking context.

questions.question: Which modern CSS property creates a new stacking context safely without requiring position or z-index hacks?
questions.explanation: isolation: isolate creates a new stacking context on the element without altering its position coordinates.

questions.question: Which of the following unexpected properties creates a new stacking context as a side effect?
questions.hint: Opacity and CSS transforms trigger stacking contexts.
questions.explanation: Properties like opacity < 1, transform, filter, and clip-path create a new stacking context.

questions.question: What happens if two positioned sibling elements with the same z-index value overlap?
options: The one that appears later in the HTML source code renders on top
The one with the shorter ID renders on top
questions.explanation: When z-index values are identical within the same stacking context, natural source order decides: the later element stacks on top.
